questions.worked_solution:
At $x=-4,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-{4}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,-{4}^{-}}({x}^{2}+3x) \\  & =(-4)^{2}+3(-4) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-{4}^{+}}f(x)=-5a.
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-4,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-{4}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,-{4}^{+}}f(x) \\ 4 & =-5a \\ a & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-4$ for $a=-\frac{4}{5}.$

questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{x+1}=\frac{(-1)^{2}-1}{-1+1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{x+1} & =\frac{(x+1)(x-1)}{x+1} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x+1)}(x-1)}{\cancel{x+1}} \\  & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,-1}\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{x+1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,-1}(x-1) \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

First, as $x\to \infty ,$ we can assume that $x>-1.$ So, we use the following expression for $f(x):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{x+1}
$$

Now, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can evaluate the resulting expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{x}-\frac{1}{x})}{(\frac{x}{x}+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(x-\frac{1}{x})}{(1+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x-0}{1+0} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }x \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

and

questions.worked_solution:
A function is not differentiable wherever it has a discontinuity, corner, cusp, or vertical tangent.

* At $x=-4$ the function has a corner point, so it's not differentiable there.

* At $x=-2$ the function has a jump discontinuity, so it's not differentiable there.

Of these two points, $f(x)$ is continuous only at $x=-4.$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x=-4.$

The extreme value theorem states the following:

> *If $f(x)$ is a continuous function defined on the closed interval $[a,b],$ then $f(x)$ always has at least one global maximum and one global minimum on $[a,b]$*.

So, the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

The smallest possible integer $h$ such that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[h,3]$ is $h=-1,$ as shown below.

questions.worked_solution:
First, comparing

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-5}\frac{f(x)-f(-5)}{x-(-5)}
$$

with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change,

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{x\to \,a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a},
$$

we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-5}\frac{f(x)-f(-5)}{x-(-5)}={f}^{′}(-5).
$$

Now, computing the derivative of $f$ for $x<-1,$ we have 

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=2x+3,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(-5)=2(-5)+3=-7.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-5}\frac{f(x)-f(-5)}{x-(-5)}=-7.
$$
